title: Sound and Pitch
intro: Music is organised sound. Before naming notes and chords it helps to know what a musical sound is: a vibration with a frequency we hear as pitch, an amplitude we hear as loudness, and a mixture of partials we hear as tone colour.

blocks.text: A sound is a pressure wave

A vibrating string, reed or air column pushes the air around it back and forth. The pressure changes travel outward at about 343 m/s and move your eardrum. A musical tone is a vibration that repeats regularly; noise does not repeat.

The number of repetitions per second is the frequency, measured in hertz (Hz). We hear frequency as pitch: higher frequency, higher pitch. Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; the piano runs from A0 = 27.5 Hz to C8 ≈ 4186 Hz.

Pitch perception is logarithmic. Doubling the frequency always sounds like the same step, the octave, whether it is 110 → 220 Hz or 1760 → 3520 Hz. That is why notes an octave apart share a name: A2, A3, A4 and A5 are 110, 220, 440 and 880 Hz.

blocks.caption: Equal-tempered frequency of MIDI note n; A4 is note 69 and middle C (C4) is note 60.

blocks.text: The octave is divided into 12 equal semitones on a modern keyboard, so each semitone multiplies the frequency by $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$. To compare pitches finely we use cents: 100 cents per semitone, 1200 per octave.

The size of the pressure swing is the amplitude. Loudness grows roughly with the logarithm of the sound's intensity, which is why it is measured in decibels: every 10 dB is ten times the intensity and sounds roughly twice as loud. Musicians write loudness as dynamics, from pp (pianissimo, very soft) through p, mp, mf and f to ff (fortissimo, very loud).
Timbre is the mixture of partials

A violin and a flute playing the same A4 have the same frequency and can have the same loudness, yet sound different. The difference is timbre (tone colour). Almost every pitched instrument vibrates at many frequencies at once: the fundamental, which sets the pitch, and partials above it. For strings and winds those partials sit at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, the harmonic series, which the next page explores. How strong each partial is, and how the mixture changes as the note starts and decays, makes the timbre.

blocks.title: Octaves
blocks.text: A note is at 196 Hz. What are the frequencies of the notes one and two octaves above it?
solution: Each octave doubles the frequency: 196 × 2 = 392 Hz, and 392 × 2 = 784 Hz. (These are G3, G4 and G5.)

blocks.title: Cents
blocks.text: How many cents is the interval from 440 Hz to 660 Hz?
solution: cents = 1200 × log2(660/440) = 1200 × log2(1.5) = 1200 × 0.58496 ≈ 702.0 cents. That is a pure perfect fifth, about 2 cents wider than an equal-tempered fifth (700 cents).
